ground_truth_witness: n = 3, m = 5, so S = {5, 6, 7}. The lemma's hypothesis holds: S contains a multiple of 1 (5, 6, 7), a multiple of 2 (6), and a multiple of 3 (6). But the proof's regrouping requires a ONE-TO-ONE assignment of the three elements to the factors 1, 2, 3 with each element divisible by its assigned factor, and no such assignment exists: the factor set T = {2, 3} needs 2 distinct elements, yet the only element of S divisible by 2 or by 3 is the single element 6 (|T| = 2 > 1 = |N(T)|, a Hall violation). The script also checks all 3! = 6 permutations directly and finds 0 valid assignments. Hence 5*6*7 cannot be written as (k_1*1)(k_2*2)(k_3*3) with the k_i arising from a matching of the elements of S. The theorem itself remains true (5*6*7 = 210 = 6 * 35, so 3! divides the product); what is refuted is precisely the proof's regrouping step. This is the lexicographically smallest counterexample in (n, m); failures are generic, e.g. every m ≡ 5 (mod 6) fails at n = 3, and 35,319 of the 60,000 searched pairs fail overall.
ground_truth_flaw: The proof claims that because S = {m, m+1, ..., m+n-1} contains a multiple of j for each j = 1..n, the product of the elements of S can be regrouped as (k_1 * 1)(k_2 * 2)...(k_n * n), i.e. the n elements of S can be matched one-to-one with the factors 1, 2, ..., n so that each element is a multiple of its assigned factor. This simultaneous/distinct-representative regrouping does not follow from the cited lemma and is false in general.
